en: Points of Controversy:
The Chapter on Latent Dispositions,
Fifteenth Section.
Is conditionality determined? Yes.
Is it not the case that investigation is a cause and it is also a predominance-condition? Yes.
If investigation is a cause and it is also a predominance-condition, then indeed, you must say this:
“It is a condition by way of root-condition; it is a condition by way of predominance-condition.
Is it not the case that desire-predominance is the predominance of co-nascent states?
Yes, it is.
If desire as a dominant factor is the dominant condition for co-nascent states, then indeed it must be said:
"It is a condition by way of the dominant condition; it is a condition by way of the co-nascence condition.
Is it not the case that energy as a dominant factor is the dominant condition for co-nascent states?
“Yes.
“If energy as the dominant factor is the dominant condition for co-nascent states, then indeed it must be said:
‘It is a condition by way of the dominant condition; it is a condition by way of the co-nascence condition.’”
Is it not the case that energy is the dominant factor over its co-nascent states, and that it is also a faculty?
Yes, it is.
If energy is the dominant factor over its co-nascent states and it is also a faculty, then indeed, you must admit this.
“[It is] a condition by way of predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya), [it is] a condition by way of faculty-condition (indriyapaccaya).
Is it not the case that energy-predominance (vīriyādhipati) is the predominance of co-nascent states, and that it is also a path-factor (maggaṅga)?
Yes, it is.
If energy as a dominant factor is the dominant influence over its co-nascent states and is a path factor, then indeed it should be said:
"It is a condition by way of dominance-condition and a condition by way of path-condition.
Is it not the case that mind as a dominant factor is the dominant influence over its co-nascent states?
Yes. If mental predominance is a predominance for co-nascent states, then indeed it must be said:
"It is a condition by way of the predominance condition; it is a condition by way of the co-nascence condition."
Is it not the case that mind is the dominant factor for co-nascent states, and that it is also nutriment? Yes.
If mind is the dominant factor for co-nascent states and it is also nutriment, then indeed, it must be said:
“[It is] a condition by way of predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya), a condition by way of nutriment-condition (āhārapaccaya).
Is it not the case that mental predominance (cittādhipati) is the predominance of co-nascent states, and that it is also a faculty (indriya)?
Yes, it is.
If mental dominance (*cittādhipati*) is the dominant factor for co-nascent states and is also a faculty (*indriya*), then indeed, O friend, it should be said:
"It is a condition by way of the dominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*); it is a condition by way of the faculty condition (*indriyapaccaya*).
Is it not the case that investigative dominance (*vīmaṁsādhipati*) is the dominant factor for co-nascent states?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “If the predominance of investigation (vīmaṁsādhipati) is a predominance-condition for co-nascent states, then indeed it must be said:
‘It is a condition by way of predominance-condition and a condition by way of co-nascence-condition.’”
Is it not the case that investigation (vīmaṁsā) is the dominant factor over its co-nascent states and is also a faculty?
Yes, it is.
If investigation is the dominant factor over its co-nascent states and is also a faculty, then indeed, it must be said:
“It is a condition by way of predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya); it is a condition by way of faculty-condition (indriyapaccaya).
Is it not the case that investigation-predominance (vīmaṁsādhipati) is a predominance for co-nascent states, and that it is also a path-factor (maggaṅga)?
Yes, it is.
If investigation is the dominant factor for its co-nascent states and is a path-factor, then indeed it should be said:
“It is a condition by way of the dominance-condition; it is a condition by way of the path-condition.
Is it not the case that reflection arises having made the noble state an object, and that [noble state] is its object-condition?
“Yes.
“If, having held the noble Dhamma in high esteem, review-knowledge arises, and that [Dhamma] is its object, then indeed, sir, it should be said:
‘It is a condition by way of predominance-condition and a condition by way of object-condition.’”
Is it not the case that preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding wholesome states by way of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and that this is also repetition (*āsevana*)?
Yes.
If preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding wholesome states by way of proximity-condition, and that is repetition, then indeed, O friend, you must say:
“It is a condition by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), it is a condition by way of repetition-condition (āsevana-paccaya).
Is it not the case that preceding unwholesome states are a condition for succeeding unwholesome states by way of proximity-condition, and that [proximity] is also repetition?
Yes, it is.

If preceding unwholesome states are a condition for succeeding unwholesome states by way of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and that is also repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), then indeed, it should be said:
"It is a condition by way of proximity-condition and a condition by way of repetition-condition.

Is it not the case that preceding functional-ineffective states (*kiriya-abyākata*) are a condition for succeeding functional-ineffective states by way of proximity-condition and that is also repetition?
“Yes.

“If it is true that preceding functional-indeterminate states are a condition for succeeding functional-indeterminate states by way of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and that this is also repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*), then indeed, sir, it must be said:
‘It is a condition by way of proximity-condition and a condition by way of repetition-condition.’”
Is it not to be said that "conditionality is determined"?
Yes, it is.

"It is a condition by way of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya), it is a condition by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), it is a condition by way of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), and it is a condition by way of the contiguity-condition (samanantara-paccaya)"—
this should not be said. Therefore,
the nature of conditions is indeed determined.
The Discussion on Conditionality is concluded.
